isolation_requirement: 200 feet from sh2 (supersweet) varieties OR stagger planting 10+ days
disease_resistance: Resistant to Southern Leaf Blight, Northern Leaf Blight, and Stewart's Wilt
variety_notes: Released 1955; set the standard for white sweet corn. Late-season variety. Tender, small, creamy-white kernels with old-fashioned corny flavor. 14-16 rows on 8-9 inch ears. Tight husks help keep corn worms to a minimum. CRITICAL: su corn converts sugars to starch quickly at ambient temperature; cool ears immediately after harvest. Best for fresh use within 3-5 days. Freezes well. Treated seed (fungicide coating) is standard for commercial packets — check package if organic is required.
sources: Gurney's; Territorial Seed; Hancock Seed; Holmes Seed; John Scheepers; Pinetree; HOSS; True Leaf Market; Ferry-Morse
source_notes: Days-to-maturity ranges 84-92 across sources based on climate; used 88-92 as most common. Planting in blocks (not rows) is essential for wind pollination — every source emphasizes this.

isolation_requirement: 1 mile from other corn varieties OR staggered timing (10+ days) OR caging
use_types: flour/cornmeal (primary); fresh roasting at milk stage; ornamental
disease_resistance: Drought tolerant; cold tolerant; wind tolerant; vigorous at high altitudes and in short-season climates
variety_notes: Bred by Dave Christensen in Big Timber, Montana since 1970. Developed from 70-100 Native American heirloom corns. Multi-colored kernels in gold, orange, red, pink, blue, purple, white, and maroon — every ear is different. Soft flour starch grinds easily (unlike flint). 13% protein, exceptional for open-pollinated corn. Rich in anthocyanins in colored kernels. Often called the hardiest and fastest-maturing grain corn in the world. Leave ears on plant until husks are fully dry; picking early causes mold in storage. Buy direct from Victory Seeds or Fedco to support the ongoing breeding work.
sources: Victory Seeds; Fedco; Seeds Trust; Hardy Seeds; RareSeeds; True Leaf Market; Alliance of Native Seedkeepers; Specialty Produce
source_notes: Timing varies significantly by climate: 70 days in warm climates, 90+ in cold mountain climates. Used 85-100 as reasonable range. Sugar type blank because it's a flour corn — su/se/sh2 classification applies only to sweet corn.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from su/sh2/field/flour/popcorn by 200+ feet or 12+ days apart in planting; se varieties do not need isolation from other se types
disease_resistance: Resistant to Maize Dwarf Mosaic Virus (MDMV) and common rust; tolerant to Stewart's Wilt
variety_notes: Bold flavor for a bold name. Yellow 8" ears with 16-18 rows of exceptionally sweet corny tender kernels. Benchmark SE variety for home gardens — consistent favorite among market growers. RM = Rust and Mosaic Virus resistance (improved from original Bodacious). Can be a fussy germinator — wait for warm soil. Holds quality a week at maturity.
sources: Fedco; Territorial Seed; LSU AgCenter; Ferry-Morse
source_notes: Universally cited as benchmark SE sweet corn; "RM" suffix indicates disease-resistant improved version.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from su/sh2/field by 200+ feet or 12+ days
disease_resistance: Tolerant to Stewart's Wilt; good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Premium bicolor (yellow and white kernels) SE sweet corn. "Ambrosia is perfect for a wide range of markets, from fresh home-garden use to long-distance shipping" — per Fedco. 6.5 ft plants with good early vigor. In stressful conditions the tips don't always fill. Flavor named after Greek "food of the gods." Beloved by corn tasters — universal consensus favorite.
sources: Fedco; Rupp Seeds; LSU AgCenter; Gardening Chores
source_notes: Most popular bicolor SE sweet corn. Names bicolor types often include "Bicolor" in variety name.

isolation_requirement: For best flavor, isolate from su, sh2, and standard se varieties by 200+ feet or 12+ days
disease_resistance: Good general resistance; tolerant to Stewart's Wilt
variety_notes: 2001 All-America Selections winner. Yellow synergistic corn combining se tenderness with sh2 extra sweetness and extended shelf life. Award-winning flavor. 16-row 8-9" ears on 6-7 ft plants. Considered one of the top sweet corns by home gardeners. Keeps well — doesn't need to be eaten immediately like su varieties.
sources: LSU AgCenter; Gardening Chores; Ferry-Morse; Rupp Seeds
source_notes: Synergistic/TripleSweet category represents newer breeding combining best of se and sh2 traits.

isolation_requirement: CRITICAL: isolate sh2 from all other corn types by 200-300+ feet or 12-14 days — cross pollination produces starchy tough kernels
disease_resistance: Moderate disease resistance; plant later than su/se due to temperature sensitivity
variety_notes: 1986 All-America Selections winner — one of the first premier sh2 varieties. 4-10x sugar of standard sweet corn. White kernels. Holds sweetness 10+ days refrigerated. Sh2 seeds germinate poorly in cold soil (65F minimum) — plant 2-3 weeks later than su/se. Sh2 kernels are smaller/shrunken — plant seeds shallow. Very popular for farmers markets because of shelf life.
sources: LSU AgCenter; Park Seed; All-America Selections
source_notes: Sh2 isolation is CRITICAL — ruined crops from cross-pollination are common failure mode.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from su/sh2/field by 200+ feet or 12+ days
disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Yellow SE with enormous 9" ears and 18 rows of buttery tender kernels. Very large for an SE. Slightly later than Bodacious (83-87 vs 72). Tall 7-8 ft plants. Heavy producer. Ideal for BBQ and freezing. Well-liked by home gardeners who want big ears.
sources: LSU AgCenter; Agricarehub
source_notes: Another benchmark SE variety alongside Bodacious — Incredible is the bigger-eared option.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from se/sh2 types to preserve heirloom genetics; can cross with field corn
disease_resistance: Moderate disease resistance; widely adapted
variety_notes: Introduced by Burpee in 1902 — the variety that made yellow corn popular in America (previously only white corn was considered high quality). Classic old-fashioned sweet corn flavor — nutty, corny, not candy-sweet. Germinates well in cool soil (55F minimum). Converts to starch quickly after harvest — eat same day for peak flavor. Open-pollinated — save seeds. 5-6 ft stalks with 2+ ears each. Heirloom standard.
sources: Ferry-Morse; Wildrose Heritage; Gardening Chores; Baker Creek
source_notes: Historical significance + cool-soil germination make it the heirloom sweet corn of choice.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn varieties to preserve color and genetics; 600+ feet between varieties
use_types: cornmeal; tortillas; piki bread; fresh eating young; ceremonial
disease_resistance: Drought-tolerant; adapted to arid conditions; may struggle in high humidity
variety_notes: Traditional staple of the Hopi people in northern Arizona. Deep blue kernels retain color when cooked — distinctive blue tortillas, cornbread, atole. Higher protein than dent corn. Drought and heat tolerant — desert-adapted genetics. 5-7 ft stalks with 1-2 ears each. Can be eaten as sweet corn when very young, or dried for meal. Deep cultural significance — harvest traditionally by pulling (not cutting) ears.
sources: St. Clare Seeds; Territorial Seed; Ujamaa Seeds; Pinetree Garden Seeds
source_notes: Cultural significance important — acknowledge Hopi origin and ceremonial use.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn by 600+ feet to maintain color
use_types: cornmeal; flour; grits; roasting ears young; moonshine; ornamental
disease_resistance: Drought-tolerant; hardy and adaptable
variety_notes: Pre-1845 heirloom dent corn. Dark red kernels — gruesome name refers to color, not history. Tall 10-12 ft stalks with 2 ears per plant. Main uses: cornmeal and flour; also tastes good roasted fresh when young. Drought-tolerant. Beautiful ornamental use in fall decor. Popular moonshine and whiskey corn. Classic Appalachian variety.
sources: St. Clare Seeds; Rich Farm Garden; Thresh Seed Co
source_notes: Name refers to striking color; one of the oldest documented dent corn varieties.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn varieties by 600+ feet
disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance; adaptable
variety_notes: Heirloom from Zapotec people of Oaxaca, Mexico. Unique pearlescent green kernels — striking for fall decoration. Grinds into flavorful green-tinted masa for authentic Oaxacan tortillas and tamales. Despite Mexican origin, shorter stature (6-7 ft) and faster maturity (95-105 days) than most southern heirlooms — grows well in temperate climates. Popular with distillers for moonshine and bourbon.
sources: Thresh Seed Co; Rich Farm Garden; Sandhill Preservation; Tomorrow Seeds
source_notes: Days-to-maturity varies widely between sources (70-105) — using 95-105 conservative range based on most reliable sources.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn varieties by 600+ feet
disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Southern heirloom. Very large white kernels — among the biggest of any corn. The classic hominy and grits corn — kernels hull easily with lye treatment. Tall 9-12 ft stalks. Low row count (8-10) but each kernel is huge. Historic importance in Southern US cuisine. Slower conversion to starch than sweet corn — versatile use at various stages.
sources: Rich Farm Garden; Sandhill Preservation
source_notes: Essential variety for traditional Southern hominy and grits preparation.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn varieties by 600+ feet to preserve color
disease_resistance: Drought-tolerant; cold-soil tolerant (proven at 8,000 ft elevation)
variety_notes: Traditional Hopi variety. Kernels range from slate blue to brilliant turquoise with occasional purples. BOTH flour and dent kernels on same ear — rare. Earlier than Hopi Blue (~90 vs ~110 days). Tolerant to wide temperature swings and cool soil — grows successfully at 8,000 ft elevation. Original seed from John "Eesawu" Kimmey, Talavaya Center founder.
sources: Baker Creek (RareSeeds); Sandhill Preservation
source_notes: Significant cultural heritage; shorter season than typical Hopi varieties makes it useful beyond the Southwest.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn varieties by 600+ feet
disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance; adaptable
variety_notes: Sacred Cherokee heritage variety. Blue and white kernels — some with patterns resembling an eagle with outspread wings (the ceremonial significance). 10 ft stalks. Grinds into beautiful blue meal or masa flour. Essential heritage variety with deep cultural significance.
sources: Rich Farm Garden; Native American Seed
source_notes: Sacred ceremonial significance to Cherokee Nation — important to acknowledge origin.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn by 600+ feet
disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Iowa heirloom, regionally adapted Midwest variety. Deep yellow-orange with reddish cast. Nicely formed ears on 8-9 ft plants. Excellent for cornmeal, grits, and traditional whiskey distilling. Reliable open-pollinated dent corn for central US.
sources: Sandhill Preservation
source_notes: Classic Iowa heirloom — excellent for Midwest growers.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn varieties by 500+ feet or 1/4 mile to preserve color genetics
disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance; requires high nitrogen
variety_notes: Bred by part-Cherokee farmer Carl Barnes over decades through careful selection of native varieties. Brilliant glossy jewel-toned kernels in every color of the rainbow — no two ears alike. Popular for ornamental use, but also edible — pops into cream-colored popcorn or grinds into meal. Translucent kernels resemble stained glass. Raccoons love it — protect ears. Needs abundant nitrogen for best color and size.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Thresh Seed Co; Territorial Seed; Pinetree; Hoss; Baker Creek; High Mowing; SF Bay Gardening
source_notes: Unique genetic work by Carl Barnes — cultural connection to Cherokee heritage preservation.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn varieties by 500+ feet
disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Heirloom dating to at least the 1920s. Small pure-white tender kernels with hint of sweetness. "Hulless" refers to very thin hull that disappears when popped — no hull fragments caught in teeth. Compact plants stay under 6 feet. Each plant produces numerous ears — excellent home garden variety. One of the earliest-maturing popcorn varieties — great for short growing seasons.
sources: Thresh Seed Co; Garden.org
source_notes: Tender hulless quality is the defining feature — justifies the "hulless" name.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn by 500+ feet
disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Named for its appearance — small 2-4" ears with dark mahogany-red kernels shaped like strawberries. Short compact plants (4-5 ft). Multiple small ears per plant. Pops to tender small white kernels with classic popcorn flavor. Attractive as ornamental in its natural form. Children's garden favorite.
sources: Thresh Seed Co; Garden.org; Baker Creek
source_notes: Dual ornamental/popcorn use — popular fall decoration item.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn varieties by 500+ feet
disease_resistance: Cold-tolerant; good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Native American heritage variety. Deep burgundy-black kernels pop to fluffy white with specks of color. Short-season maturing — good for northern gardens. 5-7 ft stalks. Good flavor. Beautiful ornamental use. Ruby Red and Early Pink are related colored popcorn varieties.
sources: Thresh Seed Co; Garden.org; Baker Creek
source_notes: Short-season popcorn variant — useful for zones with less than 110 day growing seasons.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other C. pepo varieties (zucchini, acorn, summer squash) by 0.25 mile for seed saving
disease_resistance: Susceptible to squash vine borer (C. pepo species); moderate powdery mildew resistance
variety_notes: THE classic American Halloween jack-o-lantern pumpkin. Developed in the 1970s by Massachusetts grower John Howden as an improved Connecticut Field type. Bright orange, thick ribbed, strong handles, uniform blocky shape. 15-25 lbs typical. Excellent carving quality. Watery stringy flesh — OK for pies but not ideal (use Baby Pam or Long Island Cheese instead). Long storage. 2-3 fruits per vine.
sources: St. Clare Seeds; Gardener's Path; Creative Vegetable Gardener
source_notes: Industry standard jack-o-lantern since 1970s — basis for most carving pumpkin breeding.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other C. pepo varieties for seed saving (crosses with zucchini, acorn)
disease_resistance: Susceptible to vine borer; moderate powdery mildew resistance
variety_notes: Classic pie pumpkins. 6-8 lb small round orange pumpkins with sweet dense flesh. "Small Sugar" (alias Sugar Pie) is the open-pollinated heirloom; "Baby Pam" is an improved modern hybrid version. Deep orange fine-textured flesh ideal for pies, purees, and canning. Higher yields than carving types — 4-6 fruits per vine.
sources: St. Clare Seeds; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Gardener's Path
source_notes: Small Sugar and Sugar Pie often used interchangeably; Baby Pam is an improved hybrid.

isolation_requirement: Different species from most pumpkins (C. maxima vs C. pepo/moschata) — won't cross with those
disease_resistance: C. maxima has some vine borer resistance (less than moschata but more than pepo); excellent long storage
variety_notes: Australian heirloom from Jarrahdale, Western Australia. Striking blue-gray rind — highly decorative. 12-20 lb flattened deeply-ribbed fruits. Sweet dry stringless golden-orange flesh — excellent for pies. Similar to Sweet Meat. Long storage (6+ months). Eye-catching in fall displays. Different species from most pumpkins — useful for genetics management.
sources: Burpee; St. Clare Seeds; Gardener's Path
source_notes: C. maxima species — similar to Hubbard squash in genetics.

isolation_requirement: C. moschata species — won't cross with C. pepo or C. maxima pumpkins
use_types: pies; soups; purees; roasting; long storage; ornamental
disease_resistance: C. moschata has BEST vine borer resistance of all squash species — thick woody stems resist borer attack; disease-tolerant
variety_notes: French heirloom from Provence, introduced to US market 1899. Also called Fairytale or Cinderella pumpkin. Deeply lobed flat-shaped fruit. Starts dark green, ripens to rich tan-brown. 10-20+ lbs. Rich deep orange flesh — considered among the best-tasting pumpkins. Sweet nutty flavor. Excellent for pies, soups, roasting. Vine borer resistance is major advantage in affected regions. Cure and store 4-6+ months.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; St. Clare Seeds; Gardener's Path; Pinetree
source_notes: Vine borer resistance is the standout trait — this plus flavor makes it a top pick.

isolation_requirement: C. moschata — won't cross with pepo or maxima
disease_resistance: C. moschata vine borer resistance
variety_notes: Historic East Coast heirloom from Long Island. Flat "cheese wheel" shape — named for resemblance to a wheel of cheese. Tan buff-colored smooth rind. 6-10 lbs. Legendary pie pumpkin — many New York and New Jersey growers say the BEST pie pumpkin. Deep orange flesh with complex rich flavor. Vine borer resistant (moschata). Stores 4+ months.
sources: Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds; St. Clare Seeds
source_notes: Regional heirloom with strong reputation among Northeast pie makers.

isolation_requirement: C. maxima species
disease_resistance: Susceptible to vine borer (C. maxima) but somewhat less than C. pepo
variety_notes: Classic giant pumpkin variety. Typically 50-70 lbs; ideal conditions produce 100+ lb specimens. Bright orange, nearly round, smooth rind. Requires MASSIVE space — vines spread 20+ feet. Good cooking quality (firm fine-grained) — not just for display. Remove all but 1-2 fruits per plant for biggest size. Water heavily. For truly competition-sized pumpkins (500+ lbs), use "Dill's Atlantic Giant" strain.
sources: St. Clare Seeds; Burpee
source_notes: Home garden giant — AG (Atlantic Giant) is competition strain.

isolation_requirement: May cross with other sunflowers — isolate for seed saving; wild sunflowers can be a source of crossing
use_types: snacking seeds (roasted/salted); bird feed; oil (small scale)
disease_resistance: Generally robust; watch for downy mildew and birds eating seeds
variety_notes: Classic giant heirloom sunflower. Single massive 10-16" flower head on 8-12 ft stalk. Large striped gray-and-white seeds for human snacking. One plant produces 1-3 lbs of seed. Protect heads from birds with bags or netting as seeds mature. Single flower per plant — plant in rows for efficiency. Historic American garden variety.
sources: Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee
source_notes: THE classic striped snacking seed — compare to Black Oil for bird/oil use.

isolation_requirement: Can cross with other sunflowers — isolate for seed saving
use_types: oil production; bird feed; wildlife food
disease_resistance: Drought-tolerant; good general disease resistance
variety_notes: THE standard bird-feed sunflower — what's in commercial "black oil sunflower seed" wildlife mixes. Higher oil content than gray striped types (~45% oil vs 30%). Smaller black seeds. Productive — multiple heads per plant. Grown commercially for cooking oil. Most favored bird food sunflower seed. Shorter and earlier than Mammoth.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Peredovik seed suppliers
source_notes: Species bird seed — standard commercial variety for wild bird feed.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other sunflowers for seed saving
use_types: traditional purple-black dye for basketry/wool; edible seeds; ornamental
disease_resistance: Drought-tolerant — adapted to arid Southwest conditions
variety_notes: Traditional Hopi variety from Arizona. True-black seeds used by Hopi basket-weavers for rich purple-black dye — the deepest natural dye color available. Also edible as snacking seed. Single large heads on 8-10 ft plants. Drought-tolerant desert-adapted. Cultural significance — important to acknowledge origin. Seeds of Change and Native Seeds/SEARCH are key sources.
sources: Native Seeds/SEARCH; Baker Creek
source_notes: Cultural significance and unique dye use make this variety notable for heritage/art purposes beyond food.

isolation_requirement: Separate from other sorghum varieties (grain, grass, broom) by 500+ feet if saving seed
use_types: syrup production (pressed and boiled stalks); fodder
disease_resistance: Heat and drought tolerant — more than corn; generally disease-resistant
variety_notes: Classic syrup sorghum — used to make traditional "sorghum molasses." Sweet juicy stalks pressed and boiled down (~10:1 ratio) into dark amber syrup. More drought and heat tolerant than corn. Can grow in poor soil. Also called "cane" in some regions — distinct from sugar cane. 8-12 ft plants. Harvest stalks when seeds begin to turn color. Historic Southern and Midwestern homestead crop.
sources: Sandhill Preservation; Southern Exposure Seed Exchange
source_notes: Homestead-scale sugar production alternative to sugar beets or maple — fits arid climates.

isolation_requirement: Not cross-pollinated with other grains — can grow near anything
use_types: grain (flour); cover crop; green manure; pollinator forage; smother crop
disease_resistance: Very disease-resistant; outcompetes weeds; short season
variety_notes: Not actually a grain — pseudo-cereal in Polygonaceae (knotweed family). Fast-growing 70-90 days seed to harvest. Excellent smother/cover crop — outgrows weeds. Tolerates poor soils. Reseeds readily — doesn't need replanting. Pollinator favorite — white flowers attract bees. Groats ground into gluten-free flour for pancakes, soba noodles, kasha. Frost-tender — plant after frost. Dual use as cover crop or grain — homestead classic.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; High Mowing Seeds; Fedco
source_notes: Versatile multi-purpose crop — worth growing even without intent to harvest grain.

crop_type: cover crop / nitrogen fixer / edible greens
isolation_requirement: Can cross with other peas — isolate from garden peas if seed-saving
use_types: cover crop; green manure; nitrogen fixation; edible pea shoots; dry peas
disease_resistance: Cold-hardy (survives zone 6+ winters); good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Cool-season cover crop — fall-plant for spring green manure. Cold-hardy overwintering legume. Fixes atmospheric nitrogen — typical yield 100-200 lbs N/acre equivalent. Edible pea shoots and tendrils in spring. Small purple flowers attractive. Plow in at flowering for maximum nitrogen benefit. Frequently mixed with winter rye or wheat as cover crop.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Fedco; High Mowing Seeds
source_notes: Standard overwintering cover crop for home gardeners in zone 6+.

isolation_requirement: Wind-pollinated grain; little cross-pollination concern
use_types: cover crop; green manure; winter-killed mulch; hay/fodder
disease_resistance: Generally disease-resistant; winter-kills at 10-20F — a FEATURE not a bug when used as cover crop
variety_notes: Standard home garden cover crop. Fall-plant 6-8 weeks before first hard frost. Plants grow 1-2 ft, then winter-kill at 10-20F — leaves dead mulch that protects soil over winter and is easy to plant through in spring. No tilling or plowing-in needed. Excellent weed suppression. Dead mulch breaks down quickly. Cheapest and easiest cover crop for home scale. Use for pathways and beds to be planted early spring.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Fedco; Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education (SARE)
source_notes: Winter-kill behavior is the key feature — plant, walk away, ready to plant through in spring.

isolation_requirement: Can cross with wheat (makes triticale) — isolate if needed
use_types: cover crop; erosion control; grain (rye flour); straw; hay
disease_resistance: Extremely cold-hardy (survives zone 3 winters); generally disease-resistant
variety_notes: Most cold-hardy of all cereal grains — germinates at near-freezing temperatures. Fall-plant as late as 4-6 weeks before first hard frost. Overwinters, resumes growth in spring. Excellent weed suppression and soil coverage. Must be killed in spring (mow, till, crimp) before planting summer crops — does NOT winter-kill. Aggressive — plan for termination. Rye straw is premier mulch. Allelopathic — some vegetables planted immediately after rye struggle; wait 2-3 weeks after termination.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Fedco; SARE
source_notes: Difference from oats cover crop: rye overwinters (needs spring killing), oats winter-kill (easier management). Rye = weed suppression champion.

isolation_requirement: Self-pollinating; minimal crossing between varieties when spaced 10+ feet
disease_resistance: Good general resistance to common bean mosaic virus; anthracnose-resistant
variety_notes: New England heirloom dating to Maine. Beautiful white kidney-shaped beans with dark maroon speckles — "trout-like" markings. Excellent baking bean — holds shape when cooked. Rich flavor. Bush habit — no trellising. Short-season maturity good for northern gardens. Classic Maine soldier bean companion for baked beans and cassoulet.
sources: Fedco; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek
source_notes: New England baking bean heirloom — strong regional identity.

isolation_requirement: Self-pollinating; minimal isolation needed
use_types: dry beans; refried beans; Latin American cuisine
disease_resistance: Moderate disease resistance; tolerates heat better than some dry beans
variety_notes: Classic small black bean — the standard for Latin American cuisine (Cuban, Brazilian, Mexican). Rich earthy flavor. Productive — 1/2 cup seed produces ~3-4 lbs dry beans per 100 sq ft. Bush habit. Harvest when pods are dry and rattle. Popular home gardener staple — stores 2+ years in airtight container.
sources: Fedco; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek
source_notes: THE classic frijoles negros bean for home production.

isolation_requirement: Self-pollinating
use_types: dry beans; traditional Native American cuisine
disease_resistance: Cold-tolerant; adapted to short seasons
variety_notes: Native American heirloom from Hidatsa people of North Dakota. Pole/climbing habit — ideal for Three Sisters plantings with corn. Unique white-and-dark-red patterned beans (the "shield figure"). Early maturing — suited to short northern seasons. Good flavor. Cultural significance — preserved by Native Seeds/SEARCH and Seed Savers Exchange.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange; Native Seeds/SEARCH
source_notes: Cultural heritage variety — important to acknowledge Hidatsa origin.

isolation_requirement: Self-pollinating; no isolation needed
disease_resistance: Generally disease-resistant; nitrogen-fixing
variety_notes: Premier edamame variety — large 2-3 bean pods. Sweet mild flavor. Harvest when pods are plump but still bright green (3-4 weeks window). All pods mature approximately the same time — plan for concentrated harvest. Freeze immediately after harvest. Nitrogen-fixing legume. Easier in US gardens than tofu-type soybeans.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Edamame = vegetable/food-grade soybean harvested immature.

isolation_requirement: Can cross with ornamental amaranths — isolate for seed saving
use_types: grain (flour, popping, porridge); edible greens; ornamental
disease_resistance: Drought-tolerant; heat-tolerant; generally pest-free
variety_notes: Grain amaranth — ancient Aztec staple crop. Single plant produces 1 lb+ tiny golden tan grains — highest yielding grain amaranth. Gluten-free protein-rich grain. Can be popped like tiny popcorn, ground into flour, or cooked as porridge. Young leaves also edible as greens. 6-8 ft plants with massive golden seed heads. Harvest when seeds fall when flowers rubbed. Thresh and winnow by hand.
sources: Bountiful Gardens; Baker Creek; Native Seeds/SEARCH
source_notes: Highest-yielding grain amaranth for home gardens.

isolation_requirement: Can cross with related wild species (lambsquarter); isolate for seed saving
use_types: grain (cooked whole like rice); edible greens; ornamental
disease_resistance: Generally pest-free; drought-tolerant; prefers cool-summer climates
variety_notes: Andean grain crop — protein-complete pseudo-cereal. Rainbow seed heads in red, pink, yellow, orange, green — beautiful ornamental as well as edible. Cool-season prefers — struggles in humid summer heat. Northern and high-altitude gardens do best. Must rinse saponins off seeds before cooking (bitter coating). Young leaves edible like spinach. Short-season variety good for temperate zones.
sources: Wild Garden Seed; Seed Savers Exchange; Baker Creek
source_notes: Most cold-tolerant and beautiful home garden quinoa — important note about cool-summer preference.

isolation_requirement: Self-pollinating; minimal isolation needed
disease_resistance: Good general resistance; cool-weather crop
variety_notes: Dual-purpose crop — grown for seeds (oil/nutritional supplement) or fiber (linen). Golden seeds have higher omega-3 content than brown. Beautiful blue flowers through the season. Cool-season — plant very early spring. Harvest seed varieties when stems turn brown. Fiber varieties harvested earlier (still green). 1 lb seed plants ~50 sq ft. Self-seeds if allowed.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Fedco; SARE
source_notes: Home-scale omega-3 source and/or fiber crop — homestead classic.

isolation_requirement: Isolate from other corn by 500+ feet
disease_resistance: Cold-tolerant; adapted to short seasons
variety_notes: Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) heritage variety from Bear Island, Minnesota. Multicolored kernels: yellow, pink, white, red, blue, striped. Short-season maturing — reliable in cool northern climates where longer-season corns struggle. Good for flour or traditional mush. Cultural significance to Ojibwe people. 8-12 row ears.
sources: Sandhill Preservation; White Earth Land Recovery Project; Rich Farm Garden
source_notes: Short-season Native American flint corn — important alternative to Painted Mountain for northern growers.
